title: Auditing II
source_note: Grounded in advanced auditing topics that build on ACC303 (Auditing I): group/consolidated audits, audit of specialised entities, auditor liability, professional ethics and quality control, corporate governance, forensic/investigative auditing, and reporting in more complex scenarios, per standard NUC-aligned final-year auditing curriculum. Deliberately avoids repeating ACC303's foundational topics (basic audit process, materiality basics, simple substantive testing).

questions.question: In a group audit, what is the role of the 'principal (group) auditor' when a subsidiary is audited by a different (component) audit firm?
options: The group auditor takes overall responsibility for the audit opinion on the consolidated financial statements and must evaluate the sufficiency of the component auditor's work
The group auditor has no responsibility once a component auditor has signed off a subsidiary's accounts
The group auditor is only responsible for the parent company's own individual (unconsolidated) accounts
The group auditor must always re-perform the entire audit of every subsidiary regardless of the component auditor's work
questions.correct_answer: The group auditor takes overall responsibility for the audit opinion on the consolidated financial statements and must evaluate the sufficiency of the component auditor's work
questions.explanation: Under ISA 600, the group engagement partner remains responsible for the group opinion and must be satisfied that the work performed by component auditors, and their own involvement, provides sufficient appropriate evidence.

questions.question: When auditing a consolidated financial statement, which additional procedure is specific to the audit of a group that would not typically arise in a single-entity audit?
options: Verifying that intra-group transactions and balances have been properly eliminated on consolidation
Attending the year-end inventory count
Verifying bank balances through direct confirmation
Reviewing the cash book for unusual entries
questions.correct_answer: Verifying that intra-group transactions and balances have been properly eliminated on consolidation
questions.explanation: A distinctive group audit procedure is testing that inter-company sales, purchases, balances, and unrealised profits have been correctly eliminated so the consolidated figures reflect transactions with parties outside the group.

questions.question: In auditing a bank, why is the audit of the loan loss/impairment provision typically one of the highest-risk areas?
options: It involves significant management judgement and estimation about the recoverability of loans, making it highly susceptible to material misstatement or manipulation
Banks are legally exempt from having their loan books audited at all
Loan loss provisions never change from one year to the next
It is a purely mechanical calculation with no judgement involved
questions.correct_answer: It involves significant management judgement and estimation about the recoverability of loans, making it highly susceptible to material misstatement or manipulation
questions.explanation: Impairment/loan loss provisioning relies heavily on subjective estimates of future recoverability, which increases inherent risk and requires the auditor to critically challenge management's assumptions.

questions.question: In the audit of an insurance company, the valuation of 'technical/insurance claims reserves' is a specialised area primarily because of what?
options: It requires actuarial estimation of future claims liabilities, often needing the auditor to use or evaluate the work of an actuarial expert
Insurance companies do not report any liabilities in their financial statements
Claims reserves are always a fixed statutory percentage of premium income with no estimation required
Claims reserves are never material to an insurer's financial statements
questions.correct_answer: It requires actuarial estimation of future claims liabilities, often needing the auditor to use or evaluate the work of an actuarial expert
questions.explanation: Estimating outstanding and incurred-but-not-reported claims requires specialised actuarial judgement, so auditors commonly rely on the work of an actuarial expert under ISA 620 when auditing this balance.

questions.question: When auditing a not-for-profit organisation (NGO), which of the following is a distinctive audit consideration compared to a typical commercial company?
options: Verifying that restricted donor funds have been applied strictly in accordance with the terms and conditions attached by the donor
Confirming trade receivables balances with major customers
Reviewing the calculation of earnings per share
Testing the calculation of corporation tax on trading profit
questions.correct_answer: Verifying that restricted donor funds have been applied strictly in accordance with the terms and conditions attached by the donor
questions.explanation: NGOs often receive restricted grants that must be used only for specified purposes, so compliance with donor restrictions is a key audit focus not typically present in a standard commercial audit.

questions.question: What is a distinguishing feature of public sector audit compared to private sector external audit?
options: Public sector audit often extends beyond financial statement opinion to include assessing regularity, propriety, and value-for-money (economy, efficiency, effectiveness) in the use of public funds
Public sector audit never involves an examination of financial records
Public sector auditors are appointed by the entity's own management rather than an independent authority
Public sector entities are exempt from any external audit requirement
questions.correct_answer: Public sector audit often extends beyond financial statement opinion to include assessing regularity, propriety, and value-for-money (economy, efficiency, effectiveness) in the use of public funds
questions.explanation: Public sector auditors, such as the Auditor-General, typically have a broader mandate covering compliance, propriety, and performance/value-for-money, beyond the standard true-and-fair opinion.

questions.question: What is the primary distinction between a statutory financial statement audit and a 'forensic audit' (fraud investigation)?
options: A forensic audit is a focused investigation specifically aimed at detecting, proving, and quantifying suspected fraud, often for use as evidence, whereas a statutory audit gives a general opinion on the fairness of financial statements as a whole
A forensic audit is required by law every year for all companies, while the statutory audit is optional
A forensic audit never involves the examination of financial records
There is no practical difference between the two types of engagement
questions.correct_answer: A forensic audit is a focused investigation specifically aimed at detecting, proving, and quantifying suspected fraud, often for use as evidence, whereas a statutory audit gives a general opinion on the fairness of financial statements as a whole
questions.explanation: Forensic auditing is investigative in nature, targeted at specific suspected wrongdoing and often intended to support legal proceedings, unlike the broader, opinion-based statutory audit.

questions.question: In forensic accounting, what does the 'fraud triangle' identify as the three conditions typically present when fraud occurs?
options: Pressure (incentive), opportunity, and rationalisation
Materiality, evidence, and independence
Inherent risk, control risk, and detection risk
Revenue, expenses, and profit
questions.correct_answer: Pressure (incentive), opportunity, and rationalisation
questions.explanation: The fraud triangle, developed from criminologist Donald Cressey's work, identifies pressure, opportunity, and rationalisation as the three elements commonly present when an individual commits fraud.

questions.question: What is 'due diligence' in the context of a corporate acquisition?
options: An investigative review of a target company's financial, legal, operational, and commercial affairs, performed on behalf of a prospective buyer or investor before completing a transaction
A routine annual statutory audit required of all companies
The process of liquidating a company's assets on dissolution
A tax return filed after a merger is completed
questions.correct_answer: An investigative review of a target company's financial, legal, operational, and commercial affairs, performed on behalf of a prospective buyer or investor before completing a transaction
questions.explanation: Due diligence is a pre-transaction investigation designed to verify facts, identify risks, and support the pricing and terms of an acquisition or investment, distinct from a recurring statutory audit.

questions.question: In the landmark English case Caparo Industries plc v Dickman, what key principle regarding auditors' liability for negligence to third parties was established?
options: An auditor generally does not owe a duty of care to third parties who rely on audited accounts for purposes (such as making a takeover bid) beyond the purpose for which the accounts were prepared, absent a special relationship
An auditor owes an unlimited duty of care to every possible reader of the audited financial statements
An auditor can never be held liable for negligence under any circumstances
Only the company's directors, and never the auditor, can be sued for a misleading set of accounts
questions.correct_answer: An auditor generally does not owe a duty of care to third parties who rely on audited accounts for purposes (such as making a takeover bid) beyond the purpose for which the accounts were prepared, absent a special relationship
questions.explanation: Caparo established the 'proximity' test, limiting an auditor's duty of care primarily to the company and its shareholders as a body for the statutory purpose of the audit, not to any third party who happens to rely on the accounts.

questions.question: What is the key auditing principle illustrated by the historic Kingston Cotton Mill Co case, often summarised as the auditor being a 'watchdog, not a bloodhound'?
options: An auditor is entitled to rely on the honesty of management and is not required to approach every transaction with automatic suspicion of fraud, provided reasonable care and skill are exercised
An auditor must personally investigate every employee for potential criminal wrongdoing
An auditor bears no responsibility whatsoever for detecting fraud, even where obvious red flags are ignored
An auditor is legally required to guarantee that financial statements are completely free of fraud
questions.correct_answer: An auditor is entitled to rely on the honesty of management and is not required to approach every transaction with automatic suspicion of fraud, provided reasonable care and skill are exercised
questions.explanation: The case established that while auditors must exercise reasonable skill and care, they are not expected to assume dishonesty on the part of management without cause; modern professional scepticism has since evolved this standard further.

questions.question: What must a plaintiff generally prove to succeed in a professional negligence claim against an auditor?
options: That the auditor owed a duty of care, breached that duty by failing to exercise reasonable skill and care, and that the breach caused the plaintiff to suffer a quantifiable loss
Only that the company's share price fell after the audit report was issued
Only that the auditor was paid an audit fee
That the auditor is a member of a professional accountancy body
questions.correct_answer: That the auditor owed a duty of care, breached that duty by failing to exercise reasonable skill and care, and that the breach caused the plaintiff to suffer a quantifiable loss
questions.explanation: A successful negligence claim requires proof of duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and resulting quantifiable damage — all four elements must be established.

questions.question: What is the purpose of 'quality control' procedures within an audit firm, as addressed by standards such as ISQM 1 (formerly ISQC 1)?
options: To provide reasonable assurance that the firm and its personnel comply with professional standards and applicable legal requirements, and that audit reports issued are appropriate
To determine the audit fee charged to each client
To replace the need for individual audit engagement planning
To manage the firm's marketing and business development activities only
questions.correct_answer: To provide reasonable assurance that the firm and its personnel comply with professional standards and applicable legal requirements, and that audit reports issued are appropriate
questions.explanation: Firm-wide quality control/quality management standards establish policies covering leadership responsibilities, ethical requirements, client acceptance, human resources, engagement performance, and monitoring, to ensure consistently high-quality audits.

questions.question: What is an 'engagement quality review' (formerly 'hot review')?
options: An objective evaluation of significant judgements made and conclusions reached by the engagement team, performed by a suitably qualified reviewer before the audit report is issued for certain higher-risk engagements
A review performed by the client's internal audit department after the audit report has already been issued
A review of the audit firm's billing and invoicing procedures
A one-off review that never needs to be repeated for subsequent years' audits of the same client
questions.correct_answer: An objective evaluation of significant judgements made and conclusions reached by the engagement team, performed by a suitably qualified reviewer before the audit report is issued for certain higher-risk engagements
questions.explanation: An engagement quality reviewer, independent of the engagement team, provides an objective check on key judgements before the report is released, adding a further layer of quality assurance.

questions.question: What is a 'joint audit'?
options: An audit of a single entity's financial statements carried out jointly by two or more separate audit firms, who share responsibility for the resulting opinion
An audit performed simultaneously on two entirely unrelated companies by the same audit team
An audit performed only by internal auditors, with no external firm involved
A type of audit that no longer exists in modern practice
questions.correct_answer: An audit of a single entity's financial statements carried out jointly by two or more separate audit firms, who share responsibility for the resulting opinion
questions.explanation: In a joint audit, two or more firms combine their resources and sign a single joint audit report, sharing joint responsibility for the opinion expressed.

questions.question: What is 'peer review' in the context of the auditing profession?
options: An independent review of an audit firm's quality control systems and selected audit files, typically performed by another practitioner or the professional body, to assess compliance with standards
A review conducted by a company's own board of directors of the financial statements before they are audited
A review of an individual auditor's personal tax return
An informal discussion between audit trainees with no formal documentation
questions.correct_answer: An independent review of an audit firm's quality control systems and selected audit files, typically performed by another practitioner or the professional body, to assess compliance with standards
questions.explanation: Peer review is an external quality assurance mechanism used by professional bodies to monitor whether member firms are complying with auditing and quality control standards.

questions.question: What is the primary function of an 'audit committee' within corporate governance?
options: To oversee financial reporting, internal control, and the relationship with the external auditor on behalf of the board and shareholders
To manage the day-to-day operations of the company
To set the company's dividend policy exclusively
To replace the need for an external audit altogether
questions.correct_answer: To oversee financial reporting, internal control, and the relationship with the external auditor on behalf of the board and shareholders
questions.explanation: The audit committee, typically comprising non-executive/independent members and shareholder representatives, provides governance oversight of financial reporting integrity, risk management, and auditor independence.

questions.question: Under Nigerian company law and corporate governance codes, why is it considered good practice for the audit committee to include independent, non-executive members?
options: To provide objective oversight of management and the financial reporting process, reducing the risk of undue management influence over the auditor and the accounts
To reduce the number of statutory board meetings required each year
Because executive directors are legally prohibited from ever attending audit committee meetings
To eliminate the need for the company to prepare a going concern assessment
questions.correct_answer: To provide objective oversight of management and the financial reporting process, reducing the risk of undue management influence over the auditor and the accounts
questions.explanation: Independent members strengthen the audit committee's objectivity, supporting stronger governance and giving the external auditor a more independent body to report to.

questions.question: What is 'management/operational audit' as distinct from a statutory financial audit?
options: A review of the efficiency, effectiveness, and economy of management's operations and decision-making processes, rather than an opinion on the truth and fairness of financial statements
An audit conducted exclusively by government agencies
An audit that only examines the personal conduct of the managing director
A type of audit that has been made obsolete by statutory audit
questions.correct_answer: A review of the efficiency, effectiveness, and economy of management's operations and decision-making processes, rather than an opinion on the truth and fairness of financial statements
questions.explanation: Operational/management audits assess how well resources are being used to achieve organisational objectives, focusing on performance rather than expressing an opinion on financial statements.

questions.question: What does 'continuous audit' mean, as an approach to conducting an external audit?
options: An audit approach where the auditor visits the client and performs audit work at intervals throughout the financial year, rather than only after the year end
An audit that, once started, must be repeated every single day without interruption
An audit approach used exclusively for very small businesses with no employees
An audit that never produces a final audit report
questions.correct_answer: An audit approach where the auditor visits the client and performs audit work at intervals throughout the financial year, rather than only after the year end
questions.explanation: Continuous audit spreads audit work across the year through periodic visits, which can help detect errors earlier and ease the year-end workload, though it carries risks like the possibility of post-visit alterations to records.

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of the continuous audit approach compared with a final (year-end only) audit?
options: Figures already checked during interim visits may be altered by client staff before the year end, requiring the auditor to perform additional checks at the final visit
It always costs significantly less than a final audit
It eliminates the need for the auditor to review year-end financial statements at all
It is impossible to combine with any substantive testing
questions.correct_answer: Figures already checked during interim visits may be altered by client staff before the year end, requiring the auditor to perform additional checks at the final visit
questions.explanation: A key risk of continuous audit is that data verified during an interim visit could subsequently be changed, so the auditor must re-verify relevant balances at the final visit.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'letter of weakness' (management letter) issued by the external auditor after completing fieldwork?
options: To report to management any deficiencies identified in the entity's internal control system, along with recommendations for improvement
To formally terminate the audit engagement
To notify shareholders of the audit fee for the following year
To replace the independent auditor's report on the financial statements
questions.correct_answer: To report to management any deficiencies identified in the entity's internal control system, along with recommendations for improvement
questions.explanation: The management letter (letter of weakness) is a constructive by-product of the audit, highlighting control deficiencies noted during the audit and suggesting improvements, separate from the audit opinion itself.

questions.question: In auditing a complex, highly computerised (IT-dependent) client environment, what is a key additional risk the auditor must specifically consider, beyond those in a manual accounting system?
options: The risk that errors or unauthorised changes could be replicated consistently and rapidly across a very large volume of transactions due to automated processing
The risk that the client's invoices will be handwritten
The risk that the client has too many staff performing manual bookkeeping
The risk that paper-based ledgers will be lost in a fire
questions.correct_answer: The risk that errors or unauthorised changes could be replicated consistently and rapidly across a very large volume of transactions due to automated processing
questions.explanation: In highly automated environments, a single programming error or unauthorised system change can be systematically and rapidly replicated across many transactions, unlike isolated manual errors.

questions.question: What is 'test data' as a Computer-Assisted Audit Technique?
options: Fictitious transactions processed through the client's own computer system (or a copy of it) to test whether programmed controls are operating as intended
Real client transactions extracted purely for analytical review
Data used only to test the auditor's own laptop hardware
A synonym for the client's actual production database
questions.correct_answer: Fictitious transactions processed through the client's own computer system (or a copy of it) to test whether programmed controls are operating as intended
questions.explanation: Test data involves submitting dummy transactions (including both valid and invalid data) through the client's system to verify that programmed controls correctly process or reject them.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'related party transactions' and why they receive particular audit attention?
options: Transactions between the entity and parties with significant influence or control over it, such as directors or associated companies, which may not be conducted on normal arm's-length commercial terms and could be used to manipulate reported results
Only transactions conducted between two completely unconnected external companies
Transactions that never need to be disclosed in financial statements
Transactions that are automatically illegal under company law
questions.correct_answer: Transactions between the entity and parties with significant influence or control over it, such as directors or associated companies, which may not be conducted on normal arm's-length commercial terms and could be used to manipulate reported results
questions.explanation: Because related parties can influence transaction terms, such dealings carry a heightened risk of being used to distort reported performance or conceal misappropriation, requiring specific identification and disclosure.

questions.question: What responsibility does an auditor generally have if they discover, after the audit report has been signed and issued, a material fact that existed at the report date but was previously unknown to them?
options: To consider whether the financial statements need revision and, if so, take appropriate action, which may include communicating with those charged with governance and possibly issuing a revised report
To do nothing at all, since responsibility ends the moment the report is signed
To automatically resign as auditor without any further investigation
To wait until the following year's audit to address the matter
questions.correct_answer: To consider whether the financial statements need revision and, if so, take appropriate action, which may include communicating with those charged with governance and possibly issuing a revised report
questions.explanation: ISA 560 requires auditors to respond appropriately to facts discovered after the report date but before the financial statements are issued (or even after issuance, in limited circumstances), rather than ignoring them.

questions.question: In the audit of a company undergoing liquidation, what is the auditor's/liquidator's key concern regarding the realisation of assets?
options: Ensuring assets are realised (converted to cash) in a manner that maximises returns for creditors and shareholders in accordance with their legal order of priority
Ensuring assets are transferred free of charge to the company's directors
Ensuring the company continues normal trading operations indefinitely
Ensuring the auditor personally purchases the company's assets
questions.correct_answer: Ensuring assets are realised (converted to cash) in a manner that maximises returns for creditors and shareholders in accordance with their legal order of priority
questions.explanation: In a winding-up, the liquidator (who may draw on audit-type verification work) must realise assets and distribute proceeds according to the statutory order of priority among creditors and members.

questions.question: What additional reporting responsibility might an accountant have when preparing a 'reporting accountant's report' for inclusion in a prospectus for a new share issue?
options: To report on the accuracy and fair presentation of historical financial information (and sometimes profit forecasts) included in the prospectus, to protect prospective investors
To guarantee that the share price will rise after listing
To personally underwrite the entire share issue
To replace the statutory auditor for all future years
questions.correct_answer: To report on the accuracy and fair presentation of historical financial information (and sometimes profit forecasts) included in the prospectus, to protect prospective investors
questions.explanation: The reporting accountant provides assurance on financial information disclosed to potential investors in a prospectus, which is a distinct engagement from the ongoing statutory audit.

questions.question: How does an auditor's assessment of 'going concern' differ in complexity at an advanced (final year) level compared to a routine annual audit with no indicators of distress?
options: It requires a more rigorous evaluation of management's plans, cash flow forecasts, and mitigating factors, and may involve evaluating the adequacy of disclosures about material uncertainty
It becomes entirely irrelevant once a company has been trading for more than five years
It no longer requires any judgement from the auditor
It is assessed identically regardless of the entity's financial condition
questions.correct_answer: It requires a more rigorous evaluation of management's plans, cash flow forecasts, and mitigating factors, and may involve evaluating the adequacy of disclosures about material uncertainty
questions.explanation: Where indicators of financial distress exist, the auditor must more deeply scrutinise management's assumptions, forecasts, and mitigating actions, and consider whether disclosure of a material uncertainty is adequate.

questions.question: What is the concept of 'professional scepticism' as required of an auditor under the ISAs?
options: An attitude that includes a questioning mind, being alert to conditions that may indicate possible misstatement, and critically assessing audit evidence rather than accepting it at face value
A requirement to assume that all client management is dishonest and criminal
A rule that prohibits the auditor from ever trusting any evidence provided by the client
An outdated concept no longer required under current auditing standards
questions.correct_answer: An attitude that includes a questioning mind, being alert to conditions that may indicate possible misstatement, and critically assessing audit evidence rather than accepting it at face value
questions.explanation: Professional scepticism requires the auditor to remain alert and critically evaluate evidence, without assuming either dishonesty or unquestioned honesty on the part of management.

questions.question: Which ethical threat arises when an audit firm derives a very large proportion of its total fee income from a single client?
options: A self-interest threat, because the firm may become financially dependent on retaining that client and reluctant to challenge management
An advocacy threat only, with no self-interest element
No threat at all, since fee levels never affect independence
A familiarity threat arising solely from personal friendship
questions.correct_answer: A self-interest threat, because the firm may become financially dependent on retaining that client and reluctant to challenge management
questions.explanation: Excessive fee dependence on one client creates a self-interest threat to objectivity, since the firm risks being unwilling to jeopardise a financially significant relationship.

questions.question: What is 'mandatory audit firm rotation', as a corporate governance safeguard for auditor independence?
options: A requirement that a company change its external audit firm after a defined maximum period of years to reduce long-association familiarity threats
A requirement that every audit team member be replaced daily during fieldwork
A rule that prohibits any company from ever changing its auditor
A requirement that the client rotate its finance director every year
questions.correct_answer: A requirement that a company change its external audit firm after a defined maximum period of years to reduce long-association familiarity threats
questions.explanation: Mandatory rotation rules limit how long the same firm (or engagement partner) can serve a client, addressing the familiarity and self-interest threats that can build up over a long audit tenure.
